replies.user: How does an LLM actually generate its answers?
replies.raw:
It predicts the next most likely **token** (roughly a word or word-chunk), then repeats that process — each new token becomes part of the input for the next prediction.

So a 200-word answer is really 200 sequential guesses, each shaped by everything before it.

What does that tell you about *why* a model might confidently produce a wrong answer?

replies.user: I think it predicts the next word based on patterns it learned?
replies.raw:
Exactly right — patterns in massive amounts of training text.

Here's the tension worth sitting with: if the model learned that certain words *tend to follow* certain other words, it will produce fluent, confident-sounding text even when no true fact underlies it.

So what's the difference between a model that "knows" something and one that just sounds like it does?

replies.user: So it doesn't really 'know' facts — it just produces likely text?
replies.raw:
That's the key insight most people miss.

Now stress-test your own claim: are there cases where "producing likely text" and "knowing a fact" might give you the *same* output — and cases where they'd come apart?

replies.user: Then why does it sometimes state wrong things so confidently?
replies.raw:
Because **confidence is a pattern too.**

Training text is full of authoritative-sounding sentences, so the model learned to generate that register — even when the underlying fact isn't there.

What would you look for in an AI output to catch that gap between confident tone and actual accuracy?

replies.user: Where does an AI model's knowledge come from?
replies.raw:
It comes from patterns in training data — text scraped from books, websites, code, and other sources.

The model doesn't "look things up" when you ask a question; it generates a response based on statistical patterns it learned during training.

So what does that imply about information that changed *after* the training cutoff?

replies.user: From the internet, I guess — so whatever people wrote online.
replies.raw:
Close — but you've described the *source*, not the *mechanism*.

The model doesn't fetch live pages when you ask it something. It compressed patterns from that data into billions of numerical weights during training, then the internet connection is gone.

So if the training ended in, say, early 2025, what happens when you ask it about something that happened last month?

replies.user: Does that mean gaps in the data become gaps in the model?
replies.raw:
Exactly — and it goes further than just missing topics.

If certain voices, languages, or perspectives were underrepresented in the training data, the model's outputs will reflect that skew too.

What kind of real-world harm could that cause?

replies.user: How would I even notice a gap like that when I use it?
replies.raw:
That's the hard part — you often can't tell from the output alone, because the model sounds equally confident whether it's well-informed or not.

So the detection move has to come from *you*: ask yourself whose perspective might be missing, or test the model on a topic you already know well and see where it stumbles.

What would you do if you spotted a gap that actually mattered for a decision you were making?

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into an AI, it probably doesn't see one word — it sees **three pieces**: "un", "believ", "able."

That's because the first thing an LLM does is break your text into **tokens** — not words, not letters, but chunks that the model learned are useful during training.

A token is roughly 3–4 characters on average. GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of about 100,000 possible tokens. Common words like "the" are one token; rare words get split into parts.

Here's why this matters: the model never actually reads English. It immediately converts every token into a number — a kind of ID — because math only works on numbers, not letters.

So when you type *"I went to the bank"*, the model sees something like: [40, 1816, 284, 262, 3331] — a sequence of numbers, nothing more.

[CHECK]Before we go further — why do you think splitting words into sub-pieces (like "un" + "believ" + "able") might actually be *useful* for a model, rather than just working with whole words?[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and the sub-word split is especially clever because it lets the model handle words it's never seen before by breaking them into familiar pieces. Good instinct.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those token-numbers don't stay as simple IDs — they get transformed into something much richer called an **embedding**.

An embedding is a list of hundreds or thousands of numbers (a "vector") that encodes *meaning*, not just identity. Words with similar meanings end up with similar vectors. "King" and "queen" are close together.

"Bank" (financial) and "bank" (riverbank) are far apart — or rather, the model figures out which "bank" you mean by looking at surrounding words.

This is how the model handles ambiguity. The sentence "I went to the bank" gets resolved differently than "I fished near the bank" — same word, different embedding, based on context.

The technical name for the mechanism that reads context is **attention** — but we'll get to that in a moment.

[CHECK]Here's a quick check: if embeddings place similar meanings close together in this mathematical space, what do you think happens to the word "doctor" — does it end up closer to "nurse" or closer to "hammer"? And why does that matter for how the model reasons?[/CHECK]

replies.user: The embeddings put similar meanings near each other, so the model can use context — like 'bank' ending up near money words or river words depending on the sentence. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter for the current one.
replies.raw:
You just described attention almost perfectly — that's the core idea. The model learns which tokens to "pay attention to" when figuring out what any given token means in context.

Now let's close the loop with what the model actually *does* with all of this: **next-token prediction**.

After tokenizing, embedding, and running attention, the model produces a probability distribution over all ~100,000 tokens in its vocabulary. It's asking: *given everything I've seen so far, what token is most likely to come next?*

"The cat sat on the ___" → "mat" gets high probability, "democracy" gets near zero.

Then it picks a token, appends it to the sequence, and runs the whole process again — one token at a time, in a loop, until it decides to stop.

This means every word in an AI's response is a *prediction*, not a lookup. The model has no database it's searching. It's doing sophisticated pattern completion, over and over, at high speed.

That's also why it can be confidently wrong — plausible isn't the same as true. But we'll dig into that in Lesson 3.

[CHECK]Here's the key question that ties everything together: when an AI gives you a long, fluent answer, is it planning the whole response in advance, or doing something else? What does next-token prediction tell you about that?[/CHECK]

replies.user: It predicts the next token by probability — so 'The cat sat on the' makes 'mat' very likely. It's not looking up an answer, it's continuing a learned pattern.
replies.raw:

replies.user: What is attention in a transformer?
replies.raw:
In a transformer, **attention** is the mechanism that lets the model weigh how relevant each word in a sequence is to every other word — not just its neighbors.

So in "The bank by the river was steep," attention helps the model connect "bank" to "river" (not to "money") by scoring those relationships across the whole sentence at once.

What do you think happens when a model has to handle a very long document — does attention get harder or easier, and why?

replies.user: So each token looks back at the earlier tokens and decides which ones matter most?
replies.raw:
Mostly right — but "looks back" undersells it.

In the full **self-attention** mechanism, every token attends to *every* other token simultaneously, including ones that come after it (during training, at least). It's less a sequential glance backward and more a all-at-once relevance vote across the whole sequence.

What does that suggest about why transformers were faster to train than older sequential models like RNNs?

replies.user: Explain more — go deeper on the same topic. Don't repeat what you already said.
replies.raw:
The key insight is *parallelism*.

An RNN had to process token 1, then token 2, then token 3 — each step depended on the previous hidden state, so you couldn't start step 5 until step 4 finished. That's a sequential bottleneck that couldn't be broken no matter how much hardware you threw at it.

Attention has no such dependency chain.

Every token's relevance scores are computed against every other token using matrix multiplication — and matrix multiplication is something GPUs are extraordinarily good at running in parallel. The whole sequence gets processed in one large coordinated operation, not a chain of steps.

---

Here's the mechanism underneath that:

Each token gets projected into three vectors — a **Query**, a **Key**, and a **Value**.

- The Query is roughly: "what am I looking for?"
- The Key is roughly: "what do I advertise about myself?"
- The Value is: "what do I actually contribute if selected?"

Attention scores are computed by taking the dot product of one token's Query against every other token's Key. High dot product = high relevance. Those scores get normalized through a softmax (so they sum to 1), then used to take a weighted sum of the Values.

The result: each token leaves attention with a new representation that has "absorbed" information from the most relevant parts of the sequence.

---

There's a cost, though.

That all-pairs comparison means attention scales as O(n²) in sequence length — double the tokens, quadruple the compute. At 512 tokens this is fine. At 100,000 tokens it becomes a serious problem, which is why a lot of current research is focused on sparse attention, linear attention, and other approximations.

[SOURCE: Attention Is All You Need — arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762]

---

So here's the tension worth sitting with: if attention requires every token to compare itself to every other token, what does that imply about what a transformer "knows" about word order — does the mechanism itself encode position, or would it be completely blind to sequence?

replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" doesn't exist inside a large language model.

Neither does any word, really.

[EX]When you type "I went to the bank," GPT-4 doesn't see letters or words — it sees something like [40, 1234, 2567, 290, 3124]. Every piece of text gets sliced into **tokens** (chunks roughly the size of a syllable or short word) and then converted into numbers before the model touches it.[/EX]

That number-conversion isn't random. Each token maps to a point in a giant mathematical space — called an *embedding space* — where tokens with similar meanings end up geometrically close together. "King" and "queen" are neighbors.

"Bank" (river) and "bank" (money) start at the same point, and the model has to figure out which neighborhood it belongs in from context.

[KEY]Tokenization is the first step: your text becomes a sequence of numbers before any "thinking" happens.[/KEY]

[Q]
What is a token in an LLM?
A) A single letter of your input
B) A chunk of text (roughly a syllable or short word) converted to a number
C) A copy of a sentence retrieved from the training data
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A chunk of text (roughly a syllable or short word) converted to a number
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and you caught the key detail that it's converted to a number, not just sliced up. That conversion is what makes math possible on language.

Now here's where it gets interesting: what does the model actually *do* with those numbers?

The answer is surprisingly simple on the surface. At every step, the model looks at all the tokens so far and asks one question: **what token should come next?**

This is called *next-token prediction*, and it's the entire game. The model outputs a probability distribution — basically a ranked list of every token in its vocabulary with a percentage attached. "The cat sat on the ___" gives very high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch."

Very low probability to "democracy."

[EX]GPT-4 has a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. Every time it generates one word, it's running a calculation across all 100,000 options and picking the most likely one — then doing it again, and again, until it's done.[/EX]

The model isn't retrieving a pre-written answer from a database. It's building your response one token at a time, each choice shaped by everything that came before it.

[KEY]Next-token prediction is the core mechanism: the model repeatedly picks the most probable next chunk of text given everything it has seen so far.[/KEY]

[Q]
When an LLM generates a response, what is it actually doing?
A) Searching the internet for the best matching answer
B) Retrieving a memorized response from training data
C) Repeatedly predicting the most likely next token based on prior context
ANS: C
[/Q]

That's actually the most common misconception about LLMs — so it's a really important one to correct.

An LLM like GPT-4 has **no internet connection during generation**. It's not Googling anything. Once training is done, the model's weights are frozen — it's a closed mathematical system that only knows what it learned before its training cutoff.

Think of it this way: a search engine finds existing pages. An LLM generates new text from patterns it compressed during training. Totally different operations.

The right answer is C — the model is running a probability calculation across its entire vocabulary, picking one token, then doing it again. No lookup, no retrieval, just math repeated thousands of times per response.

[KEY]LLMs generate text from learned patterns — they do not search, retrieve, or look anything up during a conversation.[/KEY]

Now let's make sure this clicks before we move on.

[Q]
Why can't a standard LLM tell you about something that happened last week?
A) It hasn't been programmed with that topic yet
B) Its training data has a cutoff date and it generates from frozen patterns, not live search
C) It only knows what you've told it in the current conversation
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "bank" into an LLM, the model has no idea what it means yet.

Not because it's dumb — but because meaning doesn't exist at the word level. It has to be *constructed*. Here's how that starts.

---

The first thing an LLM does is break your text into **tokens** — not words, but chunks.

"Tokenization" sounds technical, but the idea is simple: the model converts your text into a sequence of numbers it can do math on.

"Hello" might be one token. "Unbelievable" might be three: "Un", "believ", "able". GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 possible tokens.

---

Here's where it gets interesting. The sentence "I went to the bank" has one token for "bank" — but that token could mean a riverbank or a financial institution.

At the tokenization stage, the model doesn't resolve that ambiguity. It just hands the numbers forward. The *meaning* gets sorted out in the next stage (which we'll get to).

---

So right now, your prompt is a list of numbers — nothing more.

[CHECK]Before we go further: why do you think a model would break text into *sub-word* chunks like "Un-believ-able" instead of just treating every whole word as one unit?[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and the sub-word trick is clever for a specific reason: it lets the model handle words it's never seen before by recognizing familiar *parts*. A word like "tokenization" can be built from pieces the model already knows.

---

Now here's where those numbers get interesting. Each token gets converted into a point in a **embedding space** — a giant map with hundreds of dimensions.

Words with similar meanings end up *near each other* on that map. "King" and "queen" are close. "Bank" (financial) and "deposit" are close.

"Bank" (river) and "shore" are close — but in a *different direction*.

---

This is how the model starts resolving ambiguity. The famous example: in embedding space, "king" minus "man" plus "woman" lands almost exactly on "queen."

The model isn't looking that up. It learned those relationships by compressing patterns from billions of sentences.

---

So your prompt — now a sequence of token-numbers — gets transformed into a sequence of *points in this meaning-map*. The model now has something richer than raw numbers to work with.

[CHECK]Here's the key test: "I went to the bank to deposit my check" vs. "I went to the bank to fish." Same word "bank" — same token number — but different meaning. What do you think has to happen for the model to treat these differently?[/CHECK]

replies.user: The embeddings put similar meanings near each other, so the model can use context — like 'bank' ending up near money words or river words depending on the sentence. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter for the current one.
replies.raw:
You jumped ahead in exactly the right direction — that's the core insight of the whole architecture.

---

**Attention** is the mechanism that lets "bank" look around at its neighbors and update its meaning based on what it sees.

In "I went to the bank to deposit my check," the token "bank" attends strongly to "deposit" and "check" — and its position in the meaning-map shifts toward the financial cluster.

In "I went to the bank to fish," it attends to "fish" instead — and shifts toward the river cluster. Same starting token, different final meaning.

---

This happens across every token simultaneously, in multiple "heads" — think of it as the model running several different attention passes at once, each looking for different kinds of relationships (grammar, topic, reference).

The result: by the time your prompt has passed through all the attention layers, every token has a rich, context-aware meaning baked in.

---

Now the model does one final thing: it looks at all of that and predicts the single most likely **next token**.

Not the next sentence. Not the answer. Just the next chunk — then repeats, over and over, until it stops.

That's the whole generation loop: attend, predict one token, attend again, predict the next.

[CHECK]Here's the critical question: if an LLM is just predicting the most plausible next token, what does that tell you about whether its outputs are *true* — versus just *likely to sound right*?[/CHECK]

replies.user: It predicts the next token by probability — so 'The cat sat on the' makes 'mat' very likely. It's not looking up an answer, it's continuing a learned pattern.

**Your exercise:**

Here's a sentence:

*"The capital of France is ___."*

And here's a trickier one:

*"The most celebrated painter of the Italian Renaissance was ___."*

For each sentence, do two things:

**2.** For the second sentence, name one specific completion the model might generate that sounds fluent and authoritative — but could actually be wrong or misleading. What makes that failure possible, given how the model works?

replies.raw:
Good instinct on the collocation logic — that's real and important. But I want to push you to apply it to the *specific sentences* I gave you, because the two cases are actually quite different from each other.

---

"The capital of France is ___" has one correct answer that appears millions of times in training data in exactly that phrasing. "Paris" dominates the distribution so completely that almost nothing else is plausible.

That's *high confidence* — and in this case, confidence and truth happen to line up.

---

"The most celebrated painter of the Italian Renaissance was ___" is different. Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael, Botticelli — all appear in training text as "celebrated Renaissance painters."

The model picks whichever name dominates its training distribution for that exact phrasing. It might say "Leonardo da Vinci" with total confidence — but that's a *contested* historical judgment, not a fact. The fluency hides the contestedness.

---

That's the failure mode I was pointing at: the model can sound equally confident on a clear fact ("Paris") and a debatable claim ("Leonardo was THE most celebrated"). Next-token prediction doesn't know the difference.

replies.user: What is attention in a transformer?
replies.raw:
In a transformer, **attention** is the mechanism that lets the model weigh how relevant each word in a sequence is to every other word — not just its neighbors.

So in "The bank by the river was steep," attention helps the model connect "bank" to "river" rather than to "money."

What do you think would happen to a model's output if it couldn't do that — if it could only look at one word at a time?

replies.user: So each token looks back at the earlier tokens and decides which ones matter most?
replies.raw:
Mostly right — with one important twist.

In the full attention mechanism, each token can attend to **all** tokens in the context, not just earlier ones (at least during training on the input). The "only look back" constraint is specific to the *decoder* during generation, where future tokens are masked.

What do you think would break if a model generating text *could* peek at future tokens while predicting the next one?

replies.user: Explain more — go deeper on the same topic. Don't repeat what you already said.
replies.raw:
The masking question is the right thread to pull.

---

**Why causal masking exists**

During training, the model sees the full sequence at once — that's what makes transformers fast compared to older RNNs.

But if the model could attend to future tokens while learning to predict them, it would just copy the answer. The loss would drop to near zero, and the model would learn nothing useful.

So a **causal mask** sets all future-token attention scores to −∞ before the softmax, which collapses them to zero weight. The model is forced to predict each position using only what came before.

---

**What the attention score actually is**

For each token, the mechanism computes three vectors:

- **Query (Q)** — "what am I looking for?"
- **Key (K)** — "what do I advertise about myself?"
- **Value (V)** — "what do I actually contribute if selected?"

The score between token *i* and token *j* is the dot product of *i*'s Query with *j*'s Key, scaled by √(dimension) to keep gradients stable, then softmaxed into a probability distribution.

That distribution is applied to the Values — so the output is a *weighted blend* of all Value vectors, not a hard selection of one token.

---

**Why "multi-head"?**

A single attention pass captures one kind of relationship.

Multiple heads run in parallel with different learned Q/K/V projections, then concatenate their outputs. One head might track syntactic agreement ("the dogs *bark*"), another coreference ("she → Maria"), another semantic proximity.

The model learns which relationships matter — you don't hand-code them.

---

**The thing most explanations skip**

Attention scores are not fixed after training. They are computed *fresh for every new input*, from the current token embeddings.

This is different from, say, a lookup table. The model doesn't store "bank attends to river." It learns *weights* that, when applied to any input, produce useful attention patterns.

---

[SOURCE: "Attention Is All You Need" — arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762]

Given that each head learns a different relationship type, what would you predict happens to model quality if you reduce the number of heads significantly — and why might it not collapse to zero immediately?

It's not retrieving a stored answer; it's computing probabilities from patterns it learned during training.[/EX]

[Q]

A) The model looks up cat-related facts in a database

replies.user: What is attention in a transformer?
replies.raw:
In a transformer, **attention** is the mechanism that lets the model weigh how relevant every other word in a sequence is to the word it's currently processing.

So when reading "The bank by the river was muddy," attention helps the model link "bank" to "river" — not to "money."

What do you think would happen to a model's output if it couldn't do that — if every word were processed in isolation?

replies.user: So each token looks back at the earlier tokens and decides which ones matter most?
replies.raw:
Mostly right — but "looks back" undersells it.

In the attention mechanism, every token attends to **every** other token in the context simultaneously, including ones that come after it (in the encoder, at least).

What does that suggest about how a transformer differs from reading left-to-right, one word at a time?

replies.user: Explain more — go deeper on the same topic. Don't repeat what you already said.
replies.raw:
The mechanism underneath attention is three vectors computed for each token: **Query**, **Key**, and **Value**.

Think of it like a library search:
- The Query is what you're looking for.
- The Keys are the index cards on every shelf.
- The Values are the actual books.

The model computes a dot product between a token's Query and every other token's Key — that produces a raw score of "how relevant is this token to me?" Those scores get normalized through a softmax into weights that sum to 1. Then the model takes a weighted sum of all the Values, using those weights.

The result is a new representation of the token — one that has absorbed context from the whole sequence in a single pass.

---

One layer of attention isn't enough, so transformers stack **multiple heads** running in parallel.

Each head learns to attend to a *different kind* of relationship: one head might track syntactic subject-verb agreement, another might track coreference ("she" → "Maria"), another might track positional proximity.

The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected back into a single vector.

---

Here's where it gets sharp: none of this is hand-coded.

The Q, K, and V weight matrices are *learned* during training. The model discovers, through gradient descent on billions of examples, which relationships are worth attending to.

That's why attention is powerful and also why it's opaque — the relationships it learns aren't always interpretable by humans.

[SOURCE: Attention Is All You Need — arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762]

---

A **token** is the basic unit an LLM reads. Not letters, not words — chunks that a compression algorithm decided were useful. GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens.

Every token gets mapped to a number. "Hello" might be token 9906. "Paris" might be token 13trade.

The model never reads text — it reads a list of integers.

A tokenizer splits it into tokens and assigns numbers, but those numbers alone carry no meaning. The *meaning* only emerges in the next stage (which we'll get to). For now, just know: the model's first job is to chop your prompt into tokens and number them.

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into numbered chunks — tokens — before the model processes a single word of meaning.[/KEY]

[EX]The word "tokenization" itself splits into ["token", "ization"] — two tokens, not one word, not seven letters.[/EX]

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually hand off to the rest of the model?
A) The original words you typed, spell-checked
B) A list of numbers representing chunks of text
C) A search query sent to the internet
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A list of numbers representing chunks of text

Exactly right — the model never touches your raw text again after that first conversion step.

Now here's where those numbers get interesting. A list of integers on its own is still meaningless — token 9906 doesn't "know" it's related to token 9905. So the model's next move is to give each token a location in meaning-space.

This is called an **embedding**. Each token number gets swapped out for a long list of decimal numbers — a vector — that positions it in a space with hundreds of dimensions. Tokens with similar meanings end up geometrically close to each other.

"King" and "queen" land near each other. "Bank" (financial) and "bank" (river) start in the same spot — but the surrounding tokens push them apart.

[KEY]Embeddings turn token numbers into coordinates in meaning-space, so the model can reason about relationships between words.[/KEY]

[EX]The famous demo: the embedding of "king" minus "man" plus "woman" lands almost exactly on "queen" — meaning is literally encoded as geometry.[/EX]

---

This is also how the model starts to resolve that "bank" ambiguity. The tokens around it — "river," "fishing," "current" vs. "loan," "deposit," "interest" — pull the embedding in different directions.

The mechanism that does that pulling is called **attention** — and that's our next beat.

[Q]
What problem do embeddings solve that raw token numbers can't?
A) They compress the prompt so it fits in memory
B) They encode meaning and relationships between tokens as geometry
C) They translate the prompt into the language the GPU understands
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) They translate the prompt into the language the GPU understands
replies.raw:
Close — embeddings do end up running on a GPU, but that's not what makes them useful.

The real job of an embedding is to encode *meaning*, not just move data to hardware. A GPU could work with the raw token numbers too — but those numbers are arbitrary (token 9906 isn't "more" than token 9905 in any meaningful way). Embeddings give the numbers geometry: similar meanings cluster together, relationships become distances.

Think of it this way: a phone book translates names to numbers, but the numbers don't tell you who lives near whom. Embeddings are more like a map — position carries information.

---

Now for the final beat: what does the model actually *do* with all those positioned tokens?

It predicts the next one. That's it. That's the whole trick.

**Next-token prediction** means the model looks at every token in your prompt, weighs how much each one should influence the next word, and outputs a probability distribution — "there's a 40% chance the next token is 'the', 12% chance it's 'a', 3% chance it's 'elephant'…" — then samples from that distribution.

It does this one token at a time, feeding each new token back in, until it decides to stop.

[KEY]An LLM generates text by repeatedly predicting the single most-likely next token, one at a time, until the response is complete.[/KEY]

[EX]"The cat sat on the ___" — a model trained on English text will assign very high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch" and near-zero to "democracy."[/EX]
